rv.q: Haydon resists any temptation to subvert that most American of themes: the virtuous outsider who prevails against the misguided mob. But he infuses the drama's neat, almost sentimental ending with a complex resonance that lingers in the mind long after the last curtain call.

Courtroom drama is famously gripping: a genre promising highstakes, intellectual battles and moving testimonies. But what writer Reginald Rose dares to give us in Twelve Angry Men is juryroom drama. The cut and thrust of the courtroom is over: Rose focuses exclusively on 12 men locked in a room to reach a verdict.
But with its skilful structure, Twelve Angry Man commands your attention.
Overall the verdict is a positive one: this Twelve Angry Men is a strong revival of an old-fashioned yet thoroughly engaging play.
The play still works; but I suspect we've learned too much about the fallibility of juries not to entertain a reasonable doubt about Rose's ultimate faith in the system.
Although not guilty of any major crimes against the theatre, this proves an underpowered reboot of a classic.
